beginner: Chamomile is an easy, cheerful herb grown for the little white daisy flowers you dry to make a soft, apple-scented tea. The common garden kind, called German chamomile, is a fast annual that grows about 2 ft tall with feathery leaves, flowers in early to midsummer, and drops seed so it often comes back on its own. It likes cool weather and well-drained soil, does not need rich soil or much fertilizer, and its flowers bring in bees and helpful insects. There is a second, different plant also called chamomile: Roman chamomile, a low, spreading perennial used as a fragrant ground cover or lawn. For tea flowers, grow German chamomile; for a carpet you can walk on, grow Roman chamomile.
seasoned: Chamomile most often means German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla, also sold as Matricaria recutita), an easy, quick-growing annual in the Asteraceae family grown for the small white-and-gold daisy flowers used to make a mild, apple-scented tea. It forms erect, branching stems to about 2 ft with fine, ferny foliage, blooms from early to midsummer, and self-seeds so freely that it often returns on its own. It prefers cool conditions and well-drained soil, tolerates poor ground and light frost, and asks for little fertilizer; the open flowers draw bees, hoverflies, and other beneficial insects. A distinct plant, Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile), is a low, mat-forming perennial groundcover used for aromatic chamomile lawns rather than as an upright cutting herb, so choose German chamomile for tea flowers and Roman chamomile for a perennial carpet.

beginner: Chamomile is easygoing and grows in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Light, well-drained soil is ideal, and it even does well in poor, sandy ground. Heavy, soggy clay is the one thing to avoid, since wet soil rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and only add a little compost if your soil is very thin.
seasoned: German chamomile wants well-drained soil and actually thrives in poor, light ground, so it is one of the few flowers that flowers better lean than rich. It grows in sandy to loamy soils and even tolerates clay if drainage is good, but heavy, wet, poorly drained soil is the consistent failure, rotting shallow roots and feeding botrytis and damping-off. Because it is a light feeder that thrives on minimal fertility, skip heavy amendment; the priority is drainage, not richness.

beginner: Chamomile is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Anywhere from about 6.0 to 7.5 is fine, and it even takes slightly alkaline soil, so you usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Chamomile is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry and performs well across roughly 6.0 to 7.5, leaning if anything toward the neutral-to-slightly-alkaline end (UC Master Gardeners note a slightly alkaline soil is preferred). pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus on drainage and lean fertility instead.

beginner: Plant chamomile in cool weather. Scatter the tiny seeds on top of the soil and just press them in without covering, because they need light to sprout, in early spring (or fall where winters are mild). They come up in one to two weeks and flower in about eight to ten weeks. Go easy on fertilizer and water, and pick the little daisy flowers every few days when they are fully open to dry for tea. Leave a few flowers at the end to drop seed and it usually comes back on its own.
seasoned: Grow chamomile like an easy cool-season herb: surface-sow the tiny seed and press it in without covering, because light aids germination, into soil around 55°F in early spring (or in fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones). It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in roughly 8 to 10 weeks. Keep fertilizer minimal, water only moderately, and pick the flowers every few days at full open for the best tea. Leave a few late heads to drop seed and it reseeds itself readily.

beginner: Chamomile hardly needs feeding and actually does better in poor soil. Mix a little compost in before planting only if your soil is very thin, and otherwise leave it alone. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you leaves instead of flowers and more bug and mildew trouble.
seasoned: Chamomile is a light feeder that thrives in poor soil and needs little or no supplemental fertilizer. If the ground is very thin, a modest amount of compost at planting is plenty. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, floppy foliage at the expense of flowers and invites aphids and mildew, so favor lean conditions and skip routine feeding.

beginner: You can usually skip feeding chamomile. Only if the plants look pale and hungry in poor soil, give one small dose of a balanced fertilizer. Lean soil actually gives you more flowers.
seasoned: Optional: chamomile rarely needs feeding. Only if plants look pale and starved in genuinely poor soil, give one light dose of a balanced fertilizer; otherwise skip it, since lean soil gives the best flowers.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Chamomile barely needs any, but if you feed, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: If you feed at all, a balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 at a light rate is enough; a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed favors foliage over flowers and is the wrong choice for a lean-loving herb like chamomile.

beginner: A little goes a long way, and often none is needed. If you do feed, one light feeding at planting is plenty, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.
seasoned: At most a single light application, or a little compost worked in at planting, is sufficient for the season. Avoid repeated feeding; chamomile flowers best on lean soil and gets floppy and pest-prone when overfed.

beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds, leaving sticky honeydew and curled leaves. Chamomile is otherwise nearly pest-free, and the flowers themselves bring in ladybugs and hoverflies whose young eat aphids. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles a bad patch.
seasoned: The one pest chamomile draws with any regularity. Soft-bodied sap-feeders colonize tender tips and buds, secreting honeydew; soft, overfed growth is the most susceptible. Usually held in check by the beneficial predators the flowers recruit, so hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build, and keep nitrogen low to reduce the lush growth aphids prefer.

beginner: A white, powdery film on leaves, most common in crowded plantings and warm, humid, still weather. Chamomile is usually trouble-free, so this shows up mainly when plants are packed together or the air is stagnant. Space plants for airflow, grow in full sun, water at the soil, and remove badly affected growth.
seasoned: The most likely foliar disease on chamomile, favored by crowding, shade, humidity, and overhead wetness, and sharpest as warm, muggy weather sets in. Chamomile is generally disease-free, so cultural control carries it: full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and sanitation. It is worst in the humid heat of a hot-region summer, one reason chamomile is grown in the cooler part of the year there.

Prevent rather than treat: well-drained soil, restrained watering, thin stands, and good airflow. Do not sow into cold, waterlogged ground.

beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going, then water only when the top inch is dry. Grown-up chamomile handles dry spells well and hates soggy soil, so err on the dry side. Water the soil, not the leaves.
seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and seedling establishment, then water only moderately; established chamomile is fairly drought-tolerant and prefers to run on the dry side rather than sit wet. Water at the base and avoid wetting foliage and flowers to limit powdery mildew and botrytis.

beginner: Chamomile needs less water than most flowers. Water seedlings to keep them going, then give established plants a deep drink only when the soil has dried out on top. About half an inch to an inch a week, counting rain, is plenty.
seasoned: Aim for light, regular watering during establishment, then taper to only what keeps plants from wilting; roughly half to one inch per week from rain plus irrigation is usually ample, and less in cool weather. Let the surface dry between waterings.

beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base works best, since dry leaves resist mildew. If leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep foliage and flowers dry; overhead wetting in warm, humid weather invites powdery mildew and botrytis. If you must sprinkle, do it in the morning so plants dry fast.

beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base and flowers look soft or moldy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, soft rotting stems, and gray mold on flowers signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet foliage also raises powdery-mildew and damping-off pressure.

beginner: Chamomile that is too dry wilts in the warmth of the day, looks dull, and makes fewer flowers. It is thirstiest while seeds sprout and plants are young; older plants shrug off short dry spells.
seasoned: Wilting in the day's warmth, dull, grayish foliage, and fewer, smaller flowers indicate underwatering, most critically during germination and establishment; mature plants tolerate short dry spells well.

beginner: Chamomile seed sits on the surface and must not dry out while sprouting, so keep the top of the soil damp the whole time. This is the most important watering stage.
seasoned: Chamomile is surface-sown, so the seed must not dry out while sprouting: keep the surface constantly and evenly moist through germination, its single critical moisture window.

beginner: Water the young plants lightly and regularly while they get established.
seasoned: Give light, regular watering while the seedlings establish; the young plants still want steady moisture before they toughen up.

beginner: Once established, chamomile likes it on the dry side. Half to one inch a week is plenty, and less when cool. Let the surface dry between waterings, and water at the base to keep the flowers dry.
seasoned: Established chamomile is fairly drought-tolerant and prefers to run on the dry side rather than sit wet: half to one inch a week is usually ample, less in cool weather, letting the surface dry between waterings. Water at the base to keep foliage and flowers dry against powdery mildew and botrytis.

beginner: As buds form, water only enough to keep the plants from wilting. Chamomile does not want much now.
seasoned: As buds form, water only enough to keep the plants from wilting; chamomile needs little now and resents excess, which risks rot and mildew.

beginner: While chamomile blooms and you pick the flowers, keep watering light and at the base. Wet flowers get gray mold, so keep them dry.
seasoned: Through the long flowering and picking run, keep it lean: water at the base only as needed, and keep the flowers dry to head off the botrytis gray mold that spots wet blooms.

beginner: As chamomile finishes and drops seed, it needs little or no water.
seasoned: As chamomile finishes and self-sows, little to no water is needed; a dry finish ripens the seed.

seasoned: Water at the base and keep water off the foliage and flowers; dry, well-spaced plants are the main cultural lever against powdery mildew and botrytis. Avoid overhead sprinkling in warm, humid weather.

beginner: This does not really apply. Chamomile is a flower you dry, not food to store on the counter. Use the flowers fresh or dry them right after picking. See the notes for how to dry them.
seasoned: Not a stored staple: chamomile is grown for its flowers, which are dried for tea. Fresh-picked heads are best used or dried the day they are picked; they do not hold at room temperature. See the notes for drying flowers for long-term storage.

beginner: You can hold fresh flowers in the fridge for a day or two, but they are best dried right away. See the notes.
seasoned: Fresh flowers keep only a day or two loosely covered in the refrigerator and are best dried promptly instead. See the notes for drying.

beginner: Do not freeze chamomile. To store the flowers, dry them instead. See the notes.
seasoned: Chamomile is not frozen for storage. To keep flowers long term, dry them rather than freeze. See the notes.

beginner: Chamomile is a flower you dry for tea, not a vegetable to store. Pick the little daisy flowers when they are fully open, best on a dry morning, taking just the flower heads. Spread them out in a single layer on a screen or tray in an airy, shaded spot and let them air-dry for a few days, then keep the dried flowers in a sealed jar out of the light. Only use flowers that have not been sprayed. One safety note: chamomile is a daisy-family plant, and people who are allergic to ragweed or daisies can react to it, so be careful with chamomile tea if you have those allergies.
seasoned: Chamomile is grown for tea flowers, a pollinator draw, and a traditional companion, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as for produce. Pick the flowers when they are just fully open, ideally on a dry morning, snipping or stripping only the heads. Dry them promptly, spread in a single layer on a screen out of direct sun with good airflow, and handle gently so they do not discolor or heat; a few days of air-drying is usual. Store the dried flowers airtight, away from light, for tea. Use only unsprayed flowers. A safety note: chamomile is in the daisy (Asteraceae) family, and NC State cautions it can cause allergic skin reactions or oral swelling in people who are allergic to ragweed and related plants, so anyone with a ragweed or daisy allergy should be cautious with chamomile.

beginner: First decide which chamomile you want. For tea, grow German chamomile, the tall annual with lots of little daisy flowers; 'Bodegold' is a popular type that flowers early and heavily and is easy to pick. Roman chamomile is a different, low, spreading perennial used as a scented ground cover or lawn, not for cutting: 'Treneague' makes a no-mow chamomile lawn because it barely flowers, and 'Flore Pleno' has pretty double cream flowers. German chamomile grows easily from seed and reseeds itself; the Roman kinds are usually bought as small plants.
seasoned: The most important variety choice is which species you want. For tea flowers, grow German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla), the erect, self-seeding annual; named strains such as 'Bodegold' (upright, earlier and heavier bloom, easy to pick) and 'Bona' (bred for oil content) are selections of it. Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile) is a separate low-growing perennial used as a fragrant groundcover or lawn, not as a cutting herb: 'Treneague' is a non-flowering clone grown for chamomile lawns, and 'Flore Pleno' bears double cream flowers. German chamomile comes readily from seed and self-sows; Roman selections are usually set from plants or divisions.

beginner: Chamomile is a classic, easygoing companion flower. Its open flowers bring in bees, hoverflies, and other helpful insects, and gardeners have long planted it near cabbage-family crops, onions, and herbs, where tradition says it improves their vigor and flavor (a nice old belief, though not something studies have proven). It asks for little, self-sows, and there is no plant you must keep it away from; just give it sun and room, and pair it with other cool-season crops. Do not let it reseed into beds where you do not want volunteers.
seasoned: Chamomile's best-grounded companion value is pollinator and beneficial-insect support: its open, apple-scented flowers draw bees, hoverflies, and other predators of aphids, so it earns a place as an insectary planting. It also carries a deep well of traditional companion lore, especially as a good neighbor to brassicas, onions, and other herbs and as a general garden tonic (the old name 'the plant's physician'); that tradition is worth passing along but is not formally trialed. As an easy, self-seeding annual it slots naturally among cool-season vegetables and herbs. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the main caution is its prolific self-seeding, so site it where volunteers are welcome.

beginner: Chamomile flowers a long time and brings in bees and helpful bugs like hoverflies and ladybugs. Their young eat aphids, so a patch or border of chamomile helps the whole garden.
seasoned: Chamomile's best-grounded companion function. Its open, apple-scented flowers recruit bees and aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs), supporting biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant; this is a habitat benefit, not a documented pest-repellent effect.

beginner: Gardeners have long planted chamomile next to cabbage-family crops, onions, and other herbs, saying it helps them grow better and taste better. It is a lovely old tradition, not something proven, but chamomile is a harmless, pretty neighbor that also feeds pollinators.
seasoned: A traditional companion pairing. Folk practice places chamomile beside brassicas, onions, and herbs as a vigor-and-flavor tonic (the 'plant's physician' lore). The defensible part is the pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat it adds; the direct vigor claim is traditional, not trialed, so grow it for habitat and color rather than a promised yield effect.

beginner: Chamomile grows in the same cool weather as many vegetables and herbs, so it makes an easy, colorful companion that adds flowers and pollinators without crowding them. Keep it to edges so its reseeding does not take over.
seasoned: A cool-season habitat pairing. Chamomile occupies the same mild-weather window as many vegetables and herbs, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low nutrient competition on lean soil. Keep it to edges and manage its self-seeding so volunteers do not crowd the crop.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week. Move chamomile out while it is still small (under a couple of inches), because bigger plants do not transplant well. It handles light frost, so it can go out around your last frost.
seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need about a week of hardening off before setting out. Move chamomile out young: it resents transplanting once it is more than a couple of inches tall, so set out small plants. Seedlings tolerate light frost, so they can go out around the last spring frost.

beginner: The easiest way is to scatter chamomile seeds right on top of cool garden soil (about 55°F) and just press them in, without covering, because the seeds need light to sprout. They come up in one to two weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost and move the young plants out while they are still small, since big plants do not transplant well.
seasoned: Chamomile is easiest direct-sown: scatter the fine seed on the surface of cool soil (around 55°F) and press it in without covering, since light aids germination. It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks and self-thins little, so thin to 8 to 12 in. To gain time in short-season areas, start indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant while seedlings are small, because larger plants transplant poorly. Sowing in fall lets it overwinter and reseed in mild zones.

beginner: Chamomile is in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If it had a lot of mildew or mold, do not plant it, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the very next season, and clean up the old plants. Note that chamomile drops seed and often comes back on its own.
seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following chamomile immediately with other susceptible asters in the same bed where powdery mildew or botrytis built up; rotate to an unrelated family for a season if disease was heavy, and clear infected debris at season end. Chamomile self-sows freely, so volunteers may appear regardless of rotation.

beginner: Rotating chamomile is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it helps. Plant it in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased plants at the end of the season. Chamomile reseeds itself heavily, so you will often get new plants popping up on their own.
seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast, lean-loving annual herb than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving chamomile to a fresh bed and clearing infected debris limits carryover of powdery mildew and botrytis. Because it self-seeds so readily, expect volunteers, and thin or relocate them to keep airflow and to stop it colonizing beds you want for other crops.
